clue.text: 'Do OK in exam?' 'Dunno'

blocks.note: first meaning: to succeed, at least adequately, in a test
second meaning: what a quiz contestant says when they cannot answer

explanation.surface: A worried student is asked whether the exam went well and can only shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: The two quoted remarks read as a question and a reply, but each is a separate meaning of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A student succeeds in a test, and a quizzer declines a question with the same word, as on a television quiz show.

clue.text: Plan to spend a penny?

blocks.note: surface reading: an intention to visit the lavatory, since 'spend a penny' is a British euphemism from old coin-operated public toilets
setter's reading: a payment scheme where you are charged at the moment of use

explanation.surface: Someone announces they are planning a trip to the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'spend a penny' means to go to the toilet, because public toilets once cost a penny; the answer's 'go' plays on that same sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A tariff or phone contract where charges are settled at each use, rather than by subscription, is called this kind of scheme.

clue.text: Wild Australian revelry

indicators.note: something wild is unruly and out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A rowdy party thrown Down Under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild Australian' reads like a description of the outback; 'Wild' is the signal and the nationality supplies every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman winter festival gave its name to any period of unrestrained merrymaking and partying, a general noun for wild celebration.

clue.text: Everyman on cycling trip with odour, glimmering

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself, so I

explanation.surface: The setter goes out on a bike and comes back smelling strongly.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the name of this puzzle's setter, so his name stands for I. 'Cycling' looks like a rotation signal but simply describes the trip.
explanation.definitionFit: A surface that shows shifting rainbow colours as light catches it is said to shimmer or glimmer, so the adjectives match.

clue.text: Football team runs, gets exasperated

blocks.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
taken as a verb: makes cross, read loosely here as the sense of being riled

explanation.surface: A football side keeps running and grows irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is a Glasgow club (also Queens Park Rangers in London). R for runs comes from cricket scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Several British clubs carry the name, most famously the Glasgow side, so it serves as the name of a soccer club.

clue.text: Starters of duck egg fried, potato cake shortly put in microwave?

indicators.note: starters open a meal, so only the opening letter of each word is served
made short, the word loses its tail end

blocks.note: the opening letters of three breakfast words
rosti is a Swiss fried potato cake

explanation.surface: A cooked breakfast of duck egg and potato cake gets popped in the microwave.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosti is a Swiss grated-potato cake; dropping its last letter leaves ROST. The question mark flags that thawing is only one use of a microwave.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen food is commonly thawed in the microwave, so putting it there is an example of the verb, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Islander to intone a critical review describing mineral deposit

indicators.note: to describe is also to draw a line round, so one piece encircles another

blocks.note: a pan is a scathing review
rock from which metal is mined

explanation.surface: An island resident chants a scathing review about a mineral seam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' looks like it means writing about, but in its geometric sense of tracing round it puts the mineral inside the review.
explanation.definitionFit: Singapore is an island city-state, so a native or citizen of it is a natural example of an islander.

clue.text: Cockney's intoxicating, in a whirl

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the opening H, so the word is rendered as it would be spoken in that accent

blocks.note: heady means intoxicating; with the H dropped Cockney-style it is pronounced like a whirl of water

explanation.surface: A London local, giddy with drink, finds everything spinning.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class London accent, famous for dropping the H at the start of words, so heady comes out as 'eady.
explanation.definitionFit: A swirl of water or air moving in a circle against the main current is a small whirlpool, a whirl in noun form.

clue.text: Pugs' playthings?

blocks.note: first meaning: pugs belong to the dog-show group of small breeds bred as companions
second meaning: objects children play with

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests the dogs' own chew things, but the breed itself is classed in the Toy group by kennel clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Kennel clubs class small companion breeds such as pugs in a group with this name, which also means children's playthings.

clue.text: Even so, setter is creature seldom seen

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: Despite everything, the setter admits to being a rarely glimpsed creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' means the compiler, who calls himself I, not a dog or a jelly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas is a legendary beast whose sightings are notoriously rare and unconfirmed.

clue.text: Romcom reboot 'timeless': any need of it?

indicators.note: less time means the abbreviation for time is taken away
a reboot is a remake, so the letters are made over in a new order

blocks.note: the word with its T (for time) removed

explanation.surface: A critic asks whether a remake of a romantic comedy, billed as timeless, is needed at all.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the standard abbreviation for time. 'Timeless' looks like praise of the film but works on the word 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1996 film starring Michelle Pfeiffer and George Clooney is a romantic comedy, so the title fits a one-word genre label.

clue.text: Distracted wives romance soldier

indicators.note: a distracted mind is scattered, so the letters are scattered too

explanation.surface: Wives are led astray by a romance with a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distracted wives' reads as unfaithful spouses; the adjective is the signal and the two following words give every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman serving in the armed forces is a member of the military, broadly any soldier.

clue.text: Resort trip a fiasco, I confess

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, putting the letters into a different order

explanation.surface: A holiday-maker owns up that the trip to the resort was a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' reads as a holiday destination but is re-sort, the signal. The answer is a jokey British phrase of a criminal caught red-handed.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken by a caught criminal to a policeman, the phrase admits guilt and accepts the arrest, so it is an admission.

clue.text: Much champagne pours out without hint of restraint: great work!

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter goes missing
a hint is just a trace, so only the opening letter of the next word is used
out suggests disorder, as letters thrown out of place

blocks.note: a large bottle holding two standard bottles
taken as written before a letter is removed
the opening letter, which is the one taken away

explanation.surface: A huge bottle of champagne is sloshed out without any restraint, and someone cheers a job well done.
explanation.walkthrough: The R comes from the first letter of restraint. A magnum is a double-size wine bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase names an artist's or writer's most important masterpiece, literally a large opus.

clue.text: Guides plan a descent taking in waterside walks

indicators.note: to take in is to contain, so the answer sits inside a run of the clue's letters

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Tour guides plan a route down to the promenades by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across four words, starting in the last two letters of Guides and finishing in the first three of descent.
explanation.definitionFit: A long open level promenade, typically beside the sea, is a place for strolling along the shore.

clue.text: Atop donkey is Greek millionaire

explanation.surface: A rich Greek tycoon is seen sitting on a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: Aristotle Onassis was the Greek shipping magnate who married Jacqueline Kennedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle Onassis, the shipping magnate, was among the world's richest men, so the surname identifies a wealthy Greek.

clue.text: Recipients of 'horse' in jars not happy

indicators.note: happy-go-lucky and carefree, the letters fall wherever they please

explanation.surface: People given horse meat in jars are displeased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not happy' reads as one phrase, but 'not' is part of the letters to rearrange and 'happy' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend the Greeks left a giant wooden horse at Troy, which the city's people took inside, so they received it.

clue.text: Winged beast with rising stench, regularly in rage

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
in a down-reading sense, going up turns the sequence backwards

blocks.note: British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A winged monster with a foul smell rising off it flies into a fury.
explanation.walkthrough: Niff is British slang for a stink. 'Rising' turns round both the smell and the alternate letters together.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical creature has an eagle's head and wings on a lion's body, so it is a fabulous animal that flies.

clue.text: Theatre work ... um ... non-starter

explanation.surface: Someone stammering about a play admits it never got going.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses imitate hesitant speech, which is exactly what the um is doing. Noh is a traditional Japanese masked drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or plan with no prospect of success is a dead loss, so both are figurative words for a likely failure.

clue.text: Summer in France, sun hidden, snarl up lasting forever

indicators.note: what is kept out of sight is taken away from the word
snarled up means tangled, so the letters are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written before a letter is removed
S is the abbreviation for sun, the letter taken away

explanation.surface: A French summer with the sun behind clouds and a traffic jam that never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the abbreviation for sun. 'Snarl up' reads as a traffic jam, but snarl is the material and up the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without end continues for all time, so the adjective is a straight synonym for everlasting and permanent.

clue.text: Essential to hooch, a naturally occurring liquid, primarily?

definitions.text: Essential to hooch, a naturally occurring liquid, primarily?

indicators.note: first and foremost, so only the leading letter of each word counts

blocks.clueFragment: Essential to hooch, a naturally occurring liquid
blocks.note: initial letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A description of the vital ingredient of rough homemade liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: read normally it describes the substance, and its initial letters spell it.
explanation.definitionFit: The alcohol in drinks is produced by natural fermentation and is the active ingredient of any moonshine or spirit.

clue.text: OK ... oddjobber taking year to become reliable type

indicators.note: taking away removes a letter from the word

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, the letter taken away

explanation.surface: Someone who does odd jobs settles in for a year and earns a dependable reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: Y is the abbreviation for year. 'Taking' looks like adding, but here it means taking away.
explanation.definitionFit: A trusted chief assistant is someone you can always depend on, so the idiom describes a dependable person.

clue.text: It's a flipping fizzy wine

indicators.note: to flip is to turn over, so the letters run the other way

explanation.surface: Someone complains that it's a blasted sparkling wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, but it is the signal to turn the first two words round.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling white wine from Piedmont in Italy, the best-known Italian fizz alongside prosecco.

clue.text: Noisily rise, being peeved

indicators.note: making a noise means the word is heard, not read

explanation.surface: Someone gets up loudly because they are annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: In most British accents soar and the answer are pronounced identically.
explanation.definitionFit: Being resentful or aggrieved is informally described as feeling hurt, mostly in American use, so it matches irritated.

clue.text: Scupper long tree

blocks.note: to scotch a plan is to thwart it

explanation.surface: Sink a lengthy piece of timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scupper' and 'long' look like a verb and an adjective, but both are verbs: to wreck and to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinus sylvestris, the conifer native to the Scottish Highlands, is a common evergreen species.

clue.text: Source of music in Antipodes

indicators.note: the answer lies within the letters of the next word

explanation.surface: Where to hear music in Australia and New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: The Antipodes is the British name for Australia and New Zealand, on the opposite side of the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple's portable digital player stores and plays songs, so it is a device people get their tunes from.

clue.text: Next, I reply clumsily, clumsily

indicators.note: done awkwardly, the letters are put together in a fumbling order

explanation.surface: Someone admits their next answer was fumbled.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word has two jobs: the first signals the rearrangement, the second is the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something without skill or deftness is to do it awkwardly, so the adverbs are straight synonyms.

clue.text: Goddess seen in pigsties now and again

indicators.note: occasionally, so only some letters at intervals are used

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A deity turns up among the pig pens.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of pigsties.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian mother deity, wife of Osiris, was worshipped across the ancient world as a female divinity.
